Review: Overall very good value for a HD camera that supports an H.264 stream and ONVIF.The C100 does not have any fancy features but as I use with an NVR (hence requirement for ONVIF) I am not interested in cloud storage etc. and only want a decent image and motion detection.  For £20, this provides a quality HD stream encoded using H.264 (efficient use of bandwidth and storage) and the basic motion detection works reliably, triggering NVR recording without issue.  It's not professional grade but a big improvement on my old cameras which only support 640x480 resolution.The biggest downside for me relates to mounting options.  The integrated stand is fine for standing on a table etc.  and that is probably the target use.  However, it is not suited for wall mounting despite having the necessary screw fixing holes in the base.  When fixed to a wall, the back of the camera itself is flat to the wall making adjustment of the field of view impossible. Would work okay if mounted to a ceiling but do not buy if intending to fix to a vertical wall.  It's a shame, as a little more thought in the design of the stand would have solved this.Finally. The power cord and plug are black which is at odds with the camera itself. A white power cord and plug would blend in better.

Review: While I understand why 2.4GHz is better for cameras, it makes it very hard to set up the camera if you have anything but a vanilla 2.4GHz network.  Mesh networks, most of which list both 2.4GHz and 5GHz networks under one SSID (to let devices negotiate the best connection) are unusable.  Even when both the camera and the laptop, tablet, or phone running the app are both on the 2.4GHz channel in the mesh, the app can't find the camera.But it is worse than that. I set up a 2.4GHz router, connected my laptop and table to this private wifi network and ran discover again. The camera appears on the network but the app - both the browser and tablet/phone version - still can't find the camera. I am guessing that's because it requires both a 2.4GHz network connection *and* an internet connection to complete the setup.  So there's not even a good work around. Worst of all, there are no error messages or clues as to what is going on, just "try again?"So I tried and tried again but after six hours of trying workarounds, searching websites for clues, and setting up special purpose networks, I filled out the Amazon return info; back it goes.  The worst part? This is netgear. You know, the company that sells mesh routers and wifi equipment. It should not be that hard to fix this so this stuff will work on any modern network, especially for a company that specializes in routers and wifi.

Review: First, people saying audio quality is sub par or the same as other echos are off their rocker.  I’ve had EVERY single echo from (tall) first gen, to (cloth) second gen, to dots.  This sounds MUCH better (has excellent audio separation/clarity) and is quite a bit louder than ANY other echo device.  Period.  Is it CRAZY loud?  Well no, it’s not like my other system (connected to a receiver) with two 4’ (multi-speaker) towers and two 15” subs.  But how could it be?  And why would you need (or want) that kind of volume in a small speaker?  I’ve also had Sonos “Play:1” and “One” speakers and it smokes those too.The most important thing (besides sound) to me is: can it hear you when the volume is maxed?  Unlike the 2nd gen Echo Show 2 (which can’t hear AT ALL at high volumes), it can hear you!  So, all in all, it is a GREAT device.  You can’t get a better sounding Alexa device and to get a better quality speaker (from say Sonos) it would cost quite a bit more and have a larger footprint.Also, don’t forget to adjust audio settings in the Alexa app!  I recommend keeping bass flat and increasing mid range +2 and treble +4, it really adds to the clarity.  Also keep it on a solid surface; it has a down-firing sub and needs something below it to reflect off of.  Good luck!

Review: My parents have the TV volume at two levels... loud and excruciating. You've got a volume knob and a HI-MED-LOW tone on the back. (Mine was set to LOW by default, which to the regular ear is a muddy sound and makes it appear like the unit is defective.) The volume isn't super loud, so if your intended has severe hearing loss, this may not be the appropriate model. I thought I could possibly use a power cable from one of the old dots but they all work on different amp outputs. I also have to agree that this thing needs an improvement on it’s microphone. I have this installed in my kitchen and normally have to call it my name several times to get it to respond whereas one of my shows is in the living room and I can easily get it to respond from the kitchen. Review: I love my Echo devices and have been adding to them regularly intending to have one in almost every room.  When the new 4th Gen Dot came out, I got one in Dec 2000.  The sound is ok but I personally couldn't detect a huge difference in quality over my older Dots.  The underlight is neither better nor worse than the older models.  I have no idea why the power supply changed to a much bigger one or why it and the power cord are white while the Dot itself is charcoal.  An odd choice in my opinion and the charger is harder to position in some outlet locations due to it's size and the much larger shape and size of the Dot .  None of these factors really added any value to justify the higher cost to me.  After about 5 months, the Dot stopped working.  Alexa told me she could not connect to the internet.  I unplugged it and restarted and it worked for a while but then stopped again.  I even reinstalled it in the app just in case.  I also moved it into the same room my wireless router is in to see if it was a signal strength issue but it still would not connect.  I checked Amazon to see if I could get it replaced but the warranty date was passed.  Shortly after this I saw that the new Dot was on sale so I bought another one about Mid June thinking perhaps my first one was just a bad unit.  The new one seemed to work fine up until today, Sep 6, when it did the exact same thing and will now not connect to the internet and it is also now out of warranty. To say I'm disappointed would be putting it mildly.  All of my older version Dots and Echo Plus are still working great.  I would gladly return these two new devices for two old and reliable versions.

The first was dead on arrival with the black screen issue discussed extensively in other reviews and on Fitbit's forums. After far too many hours diagnosing and troubleshooting it with Fitbit I exchanged the product with Amazon. The second watch was technically functional, but suffered from severe measurement accuracy issues and general sluggishness. It was regularly up to 55 bpm (!!!!) off from other devices, including other Fitbits. I tried several positions and tightness levels without improvement. With that kind of accuracy, I'd be better off feeling my pulses for a few seconds and making an estimation that way...The form of the product is excellent however. It fits comfortably and the band material felt good. Perhaps with enough testing, Fitbit may be able to update the software enough to make this a functional product to fit its superb form.This product was clearly not ready for release from my perspective, and I have no interest in acting as Fitbit's test development team.

Review: The really negative reviews kind of baffle me. There is no question that this is an upgrade from the prior version.I think the sound quality is great. Have you gone in to the Alexa app and individually adjusted the audio settings for the device? Went in to the settings, and naturally each of the three audio settings were at zero, so I bumped the mid range and treble all most all the way up, and the bass just one more mark. Really evened out the sound, and I got to dancing quicklike. I take that as a good omen though that I thought it was bass heavy when the setting was on zero (it was just that the treble and midrange were too).  Seems to speak the quality of the small sub in there.  And I haven’t noticed much difference, if any yet regarding the direct sound vs prior 360 sound. Pretty room filling still. I’m looking forward to testing it out with the fire cube eventually.Setup was seemless, even rearranging three other, older devices and getting “play everywhere” set back up.  The new echo had no problem reconnecting with my various smart devices, maybe took a couple of minutes at most.So, yeah, so far, nothing but good things to say. Will update if that opinion changes.

Review: July 2020 updated review:A few months ago, I noticed ring updated their software so there wouldn’t be so much of a lapse in time between videos when there is still motion in the zone. One video ends, and the next video picks up almost right away. I’m now very happy with my camera!June 2019 review:I bought two of these spotlight cameras in November from Home Depot, so that’s why this isn’t a verified purchase review....wanted to preface with that.These are “okay” cameras. I have a lot of squirrels and birds hanging around my yard, so it would be nice if there was a way to tell the camera to only record things bigger than those. We have a home security system that senses large objects when our alarm is set to “away”, so I know the capabilities are out there, but maybe these cameras don’t have that same capability.At any rate, 30 seconds of recording time is next to nothing, and sometimes the camera doesn’t even pick up movement until the delivery person has already dropped my package and is on their way back to their vehicle. I also find the time for the recording to pick back up a really long time. Like others have said, anything could happen in that amount of time.The battery life also leaves a lot to be desired. I have my motion frequency set to “light”, and the battery dies anywhere between 3 and 7 weeks, depending on the amount of squirrel activity in my yard.As far as the night vision, I wouldn’t really call it night vision. It’s a light on the bottom of the camera that turns on (pretty bright light, I will say) when motion is detected. That’s about it.

Review: I purchased this 4th Gen Echo Dot to use in my office. I already have a 3rd Gen Echo Dot there, so this gave me the opportunity to play the same material through one or the other and compare performance between the two. To say I'm disappointed is an understatement. The 4th Gen audio is tinny and lacks presence. In addition, it's significantly quieter for a given volume level (i.e., 50% on a 4th Gen is easily 25% quieter than 50% on a 3rd Gen). In terms of something positive, both units do fine at recognizing my voice, the wake word, commands, and so on, and Alexa functionality is unchanged.So, if you're wanting to have full audio that has good presence and a reasonably flat EQ curve for a normal sized room, definitely save your money and go with the 3rd Gen Echo Dot. If, on the other hand, you have a small room that has problems with lower frequency background noise, then maybe the 4th Gen Echo Dot might be better for you.Pros:Pleasant visual aestheticLight-ring is at bottom so it's reflecting off the surface you have the Dot on, not off the ceilingPower-saving mode when not in use (with a few exceptions)Easy setup/Alexa integrationMicrophone is sufficiently sensitiveCons:Poor audio quality (tinny, not very present sounding) compared to 3rd Gen DotMinimal bass even with EQ turned up in the Alexa appTaller than 3rd Gen DotCord/Plug is white even though the unit is black, so it's super noticeable (and not in a good way)Seems to have low overall volume compared to 3rd Gen DotWill only stereo/multi-pair with other 4th Gen Dots (and Subwoofer)Recommendation:If you're going to be listening to audio through your Dot (either Bluetooth or streaming), stick with the 3rd Generation Echo Dot model. There's no compelling reason to downgrade to a 4th Gen Dot.

Review: Now that I finally have the Echo 2nd Generation working, I am happy with all the features, apps and functions. We have used it so far for music, games, questions, and news. Unfortunately, though, the initial setup was a royal pain in the butt. I installed the Alexa app on my portable device, i.e. my cellphone, but I also setup to access Alexa on my desktop pc because the Alexa app would not work properly at first, on my phone. The folks over at Alexa/Amazon were very nice but it wasn't until I worked with the 3rd or 4th person that I actually had someone who knew what they were doing. Therein lies the problem. If their own tech support people don't know what is causing a problem and how to fix it, then you're basically screwed. Luckily, I kept trying and trying, and FINALLY we were able to solve my dilemma, which namely was that Alexa was not syncing with my wifi, even though my wifi was checked and was working properly. One tech said it was an incompatibility to my Android and that Alexa has known problems with Android phones compatibility, so that's when I went to my desktop pc. Unfortunately that did not work either, but I was finally able to get everything in sync with my laptop computer as the device through which to activate the Alexa and therefore the Echo devices, of which I have two. Now it's working fine. So far, in two months I have had to reconnect one of the two Echos but it took care of itself and on its own reconnected. To be fair, sometimes my wifi can be spotty, so I don't think that this recent lag had to do with the Echo device or the Alexa app. It's a neat device to have if you create and execute the "smart" features in it for your home. Review: On the bright side, the picture and video quality is much better than the grainy blobby video I get from ring.  From every other side, it is a sore disappointment.  It detects occasional motion but misses much more. I watched  an animal climb a fence and although the camera light came on, there is absolutely no video of the animal even though it was maybe five feet away.  Battery life is laughably short, lucky if it lasts two days. The camera is portable and fairly easy to attach to poles using zipties. Like most of these cameras, it is heavily wifi dependent, so a stable internet connection is almost a requirement for proper functionality. I suppose it works with Alexa, but that really depends on your definition of works.  Similar to ring, if you want Alexa to show the camera,  Alexa will need to connect,  which can take a little (or a lot of) time, by which point the event might well be over.  Then it seems to be a matter of good or ill fortune if the missed  event will show up in the feed, since the motion detection is so unreliable.  This camera might work well for some situations, but for me, it is barely passable, though I still think it is better than ring.
